video_title: Anthropic's Wet Lab, Artificial Wombs in 24 Months, and Scalable Gene Editing | MOONSHOTS Live #297
gist: Colossal Biosciences CEO Ben Lamm discusses de-extinction progress, scaling multiplex gene edits from 20 to 300+ (testing 1,000), a 24-month target for mammalian artificial wombs, and why proprietary genomic data plus wet-lab validation matter as frontier AI labs like Anthropic enter biology.

insights.claim: Colossal says it now consistently delivers 300+ simultaneous edits at 90%+ efficiency, up from roughly 20 edits that most biopharma and academia would treat as a victory, and is testing 1,000-edit deliveries.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Edit-count scaling is the capability curve underpinning large-genome engineering; a 1,000-edit success would be a step change over the field.
insights.quote: we are delivering 300 plus at 90 plus% efficiency consistently.

insights.claim: Lamm expects DNA synthesis of multi-gigabase constructs to replace multiplex editing sooner than editing will reach arbitrarily many edits, because large cargo swaps via synthesis become better past a certain scale.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Value may shift from editing delivery toward synthesis machines; Colossal has begun doing synthesis internally because few others have a business driver at that scale.
insights.quote: I think synthesis will replace multiplex editing faster

insights.claim: The first-generation woolly mouse shown to the public required eight base edits in a single delivery.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Gives a concrete baseline of how modest the edit count was for the public proof point versus the 300+ capability.

insights.claim: Lamm predicts that within roughly a decade it will be possible to engineer key phenotypes in base-level organisms by multiplex editing or synthesis and grow them ex utero, approaching a 'prompt an animal' capability, though he says DNA synthesis is not there yet.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: A decade-scale horizon for programmable organisms frames timelines for synthetic biology tooling and regulation.

insights.claim: Lamm predicts Colossal will birth mammals fully ex utero, from gestation through delivery without ever entering a surrogate, within 24 months, and hopes sooner.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: A dated, falsifiable milestone for mammalian artificial gestation, which would also be a platform for conservation and potentially other uses.
insights.quote: I I think within 24 months we will colossal will birth animal mammals um fully exudo

insights.claim: Lamm names the next major Colossal inflection points as revealing another extinct species via precision gene editing, then mammalian artificial development and gestation, plus undisclosed projects he says are as notable as the dire wolves.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Signals the company's news-flow catalysts for the coming period.

themes.theme: AI and biology: data over models

insights.claim: Lamm argues that published biology is hard to reuse because genes are named, classified and experiments run differently across mouse papers, giving a 40-60% failure rate when exact experiments are rerun; AI's near-term value is bridging this nomenclature and communication layer.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Literature-mining and normalization is a tractable near-term AI use case in biology outside small-molecule discovery.

insights.claim: Lamm expects AI in biology over the next 3-5 years to mostly run simulation and design across many experiments and suggest the next experiment, while wet-lab validation remains necessary.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Wet-lab capacity and automation remain the bottleneck, favoring lab-automation and validation providers over pure in-silico plays.

insights.claim: Lamm argues a single genome fed to a frontier model will not return a recipe for immortality; instead, comparative genomics across thousands of genomes, such as species resistant to disease, is needed, and Colossal is testing this on cases like p53 and immortal jellyfish.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Proprietary, large-scale comparative genomic datasets, not generic model access, are the differentiator in genetic design.
insights.quote: I do not think that a single genome is going to uh like you're not going to feed it into mythos

insights.claim: Colossal's Biovault initiative aims to build global biobanks with governments to enable taxa-wide sequencing, and Lamm frames the resulting dataset as the key asset that complements frontier models.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Data aggregation via government partnerships is Colossal's moat strategy; 'the data set is more valuable than the model' is echoed by the hosts.

insights.claim: Astromech, a Colossal spin-off, is building 'inflection' models that plug into frontier foundation models, using evolutionary and climate context to guide where to focus, rather than competing with frontier labs.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Positions niche-data models as complements/routers to frontier models, a pattern for vertical AI startups.

themes.theme: Anthropic's wet lab and industry reaction

insights.claim: Lamm calls Anthropic's just-announced wet-lab effort validating for biotech, rejecting the view that it kills biotech, because it shows AI companies see biology as one of the most accepted use cases for their technology.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Frontier labs entering biology is read as market expansion rather than displacement by an operator in the field; it also signals demand for validation infrastructure.
insights.quote: people see that and say oh my gosh biotech is going to be dead because it should be anthropic in their in their lives. That's not true

insights.claim: Lamm states that half of biodiversity will be lost in the next 25 years and argues this needs billions of dollars of multi-government federal funding to build species 'backup' infrastructure, which zoos or nonprofits cannot provide.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Frames biobanking as a government-funded infrastructure market that Colossal is positioning to serve.

insights.claim: Colossal announced a partnership with US Fish and Wildlife, tied to the Interior Secretary's directive on backing up natural resources, and has two more unannounced government partners plus a Dubai effort.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Government contracting is becoming a revenue and data channel for Colossal.

insights.claim: Colossal open-sources its technologies for conservation use for free through a foundation with 75 global partners.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Open-source conservation tooling builds goodwill and data access while commercial applications sit in spin-offs.

insights.claim: Lamm says Colossal's mammoth effort involves 16 different lines in parallel and a goal of tens of thousands of mammoths, since elephants are social and must be reared in herds.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Herd-scale ambitions imply large animal-husbandry and habitat needs, and relevance to ex utero rearing research.

insights.claim: Lamm rejects the idea that all extinct organisms can be revived, noting fewer than about 100 T. rex fossils exist while billions lived, and expects instead that AI-era synthesis will engineer designed life.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Fossil record sparsity limits resurrection, shifting the value to programmable life rather than revival.

insights.claim: Colossal does not use its technologies on humans and Lamm says human work needs different investors, governance and patience, citing advice from Bob Nelson that working on humans means FDA 'code freeze'.
insights.speaker: Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: Explains the corporate structure choice of keeping human therapeutics in separate spin-offs.

insights.claim: Per George Church as relayed in the discussion, mammoths removing trees would let grass grow in the tundra, which sequesters about six times more carbon than trees and gives a 2-3x albedo effect, and Church projects a 6-8 degree summer permafrost cooling; Lamm notes scientists inside Colossal disagree on the magnitude but see net ecosystem benefit.
insights.speaker: Dave Blundin / Ben Lamm
insights.so_what: The climate payoff of mammoths is contested; the investment case rests more on ecosystem restoration and technology spillovers than carbon claims.
